# urai


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

Urai is a Python library for developers who write chat programs that
must work with more than one model engine. Local engines such as
llama.cpp and hosted APIs such as OpenAI’s take a list of messages and
return a reply. Each engine names its settings, formats tool calls and
reports token usage in its own way. Urai defines one conversation
format, one set of option names, one tool loop, one streaming format and
one way to count tokens for all of them. The name “urai” (உரை) means
“dialogue” in Tamil.

Urai contains no code that talks to a model. A backend package supplies
that code. A backend is a
[`Chat`](https://vedicreader.github.io/urai/chat.html#chat) subclass
that sends requests to a model engine. A backend package contains and
registers one or more backends.
[rishi](https://github.com/vedicreader/rishi) is a backend package. A
runtime is the name under which a backend is registered, such as
`remote`. [aidialog](https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/aidialog) defines
the typed message parts that some backends use.

## Install

``` sh
pip install uraiyadal
```

Urai cannot talk to a model alone. Install a backend package too and
import it. Importing it registers its runtimes with urai. The examples
below assume that a backend has registered a runtime named `remote` for
hosted models, as rishi does.

## Start a chat

[`mk_chat`](https://vedicreader.github.io/urai/chat.html#mk_chat) builds
a chat for a model name. Calling the chat with a message runs one turn
and returns the reply. A turn starts with a message from you and ends
with the final reply. It can include tool calls and several requests to
the model.
[`resp_text`](https://vedicreader.github.io/urai/core.html#resp_text)
returns the text of a reply.

``` python
from urai import mk_chat, resp_text

chat = mk_chat('gpt-5.1', runtime='remote', sp='Answer briefly.', temp=0.2)
reply = chat('What is 6 times 7?')
print(resp_text(reply))
```

`chat.hist` holds the conversation so far as a list of plain dicts in
the OpenAI chat format. Every backend reads and writes this format. You
can pass a history from one backend to another with `messages=`, and the
conversation continues there.

``` python
[(msg['role'], resp_text(msg)) for msg in chat.hist]
```

## Resolve a model before loading it

Loading a local model is slow.
[`resolve`](https://vedicreader.github.io/urai/opts.html#resolve) finds
the runtime of a model name and the size of its context window without
loading anything. The context window is the number of tokens the model
can read at once.

``` python
from urai import resolve

spec = resolve('claude-sonnet-4.6', runtime='remote')
print(spec.runtime, spec.ctx, spec.local)

chat = mk_chat(spec)
```

[`resolve`](https://vedicreader.github.io/urai/opts.html#resolve)
returns a
[`ModelSpec`](https://vedicreader.github.io/urai/opts.html#modelspec). A
[`ModelSpec`](https://vedicreader.github.io/urai/opts.html#modelspec) is
frozen. You can cache it, compare it and pass it between parts of a
program.
[`mk_chat`](https://vedicreader.github.io/urai/chat.html#mk_chat)
accepts it directly.

## Configure one turn

Options passed to
[`mk_chat`](https://vedicreader.github.io/urai/chat.html#mk_chat) apply
to the whole conversation. Options passed to one call apply to that turn
only.

``` python
reply = chat('Explain the hard part.', effort='high', temp=0.9)
```

Option names are the same for every backend. Examples are `ctx` for the
context window, `temp` for temperature, `max_output_tokens`, `think` and
`effort`. Each backend renames them to its engine’s names. A backend
drops without warning the options its engine cannot use. Urai passes a
keyword it does not know, such as llama.cpp’s `n_gpu_layers`, to the
backend unchanged.

## Add a tool

A tool is a Python function that the model can ask urai to call. Urai
builds the schema that the model sees from the function’s name, type
annotations and docstring.

``` python
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    "Add two integers."
    return a + b

chat = mk_chat('gpt-5.1', runtime='remote', tools=[add], approve=lambda call: True)
reply = chat('Use the tool to add 20 and 22.')
print(resp_text(reply))
```

When the model asks for a tool, urai calls `approve` with the call. If
`approve` returns True, the function runs and urai sends its result to
the model. The model then continues. This repeats until the model
answers without a tool call or the turn reaches `max_steps` tool calls
(default 10). If you omit `approve`, every call runs. A tool that the
provider runs on its own servers, such as a hosted web search, appears
in the history and never runs locally.

## Write a backend

A backend is a subclass of
[`Chat`](https://vedicreader.github.io/urai/chat.html#chat) registered
under a runtime name. Add
[`ToolLoopMixin`](https://vedicreader.github.io/urai/loop.html#toolloopmixin)
when the engine returns tool calls as data.
[`ToolLoopMixin`](https://vedicreader.github.io/urai/loop.html#toolloopmixin)
needs two methods. `_model_step` makes one request and returns the
reply. `_stream_step` makes one request and yields chunks. `_opt_map`
renames portable options to the engine’s names. `_opt_skip` lists the
options that the engine cannot use.
[`Runtime`](https://vedicreader.github.io/urai/opts.html#runtime) takes
a field `pats`, a tuple of substrings that select the runtime. A model
name that contains one of them uses this runtime.

``` python
from urai import Chat, ToolLoopMixin, Runtime, register_runtime

class MyChat(ToolLoopMixin, Chat):
    _runtime = 'mine'
    _opt_map = {'ctx': 'n_ctx'}
    _opt_skip = ('effort',)

    def _model_step(self, **kw): ...
    def _stream_step(self, **kw): ...

register_runtime(Runtime('mine', 'mypkg.chat.MyChat', pats=('.mine',)))
```

`Chat('model.mine')` now returns a `MyChat`. The name contains `.mine`,
which matches the runtime’s `pats`.

## Develop

The notebooks in `nbs/` are the source. `nbdev-export` generates the
files in `urai/` from them.

``` sh
uv sync --all-extras --group dev
uv run nbdev-export
uv run nbdev-test
uv run nbdev-clean
```

The tests use scripted backends, so they load no model and need no
network.
